text: Does anyone having troubles with understanding lyrics of many songs? I don't have problems with understanding texts, i read a lot. Also i am a writer, and write not only stories, but also certain amount of poetry for the songs since i was a kid. In theory, this background should make things easier for me... But nope. There are certain amount of songs (only songs, never a prose) where i simply can't understand meaning behind sentces. Often i can get the general idea of the song - like, this one is about humanity being obsessed with violence, this one about loss, etc. But when i start to read it line by line - it does not make sense. Sentences can mean something, but do not connect, do not rely to each other. And sometimes even meaning of sentences is obscure to me. And in very rare cases i can't understand the entire song. There are entire bands that have a lot of lyrics beyond my understanding. Especially japanese ones - at first i was blaming bad translation, but AI's not can translate pretty good, but it still does not make much sense in lots of cases. I can't feel the story being told by those words, and more like... shattered echoes of the story, where i constantly try to put puzzle together but fail. I have various theories of why this happens, from being an effect from asd to me just being not smart enough to understand more complex narratives. So i need to hear experience of other people about this subject. Do you have problems with understanding lyrics, and how often?

text: Let's talk: The Shadows Bob Stanley's new book about the Shadows is out today. All of his output has touched upon the subjects that I enjoy, but this new one is really close to my heart. In a conversation about the post-Elvis/pre-Beatles period of rock you can't help but mention the Shadows. They covered such a cool musical ground between simple rock 'n' roll and more intricate sounds. Hank Marvin is easily the strongest contender for the title of the first guitar hero of the rock era, seeing how nearly every notable post-1960 UK guitarist named him as a primary influence. I remember hearing 'Apache' for the first time on one of my dad's countless compilations of sixties music. Not long after, I got a hold of an MP3 anthology of their music and it basically soundtracked a significant portion of my adolescence. The Shadows were also my personal gateway to other similar artists from that period. Through them, I discovered Duane Eddy, Link Wray, Dick Dale, the Ventures, the Tornadoes (Bob should definitely write his next book about Joe Meek) and so many others. Let's talk about this legendary quartet, their place in history, their impact and what they mean to you personally. There's so much to unpack, so I'm passing the mic to all of you here on LTM.

text: What makes certain once-loved artists become hated? U2 is a big one for me. I really like U2, and it seems so too did a lot of people for their first few albums. Then, suddenly, it became like the cool de facto thing to do, to hate on U2. What was it in their case that turned them from once-loved to so widely hated, the butt of countless jokes? Was it the Africa/activism stuff? Weird thing to hate on, imo. Was it the iPod/iPhone forced-download thing? Is it such an inconvenience to delete an album off your device that it'd forever negatively taint their reputation? Personally, I thoroughly enjoyed everything until How To Dismantle An Atomic Bomb - actually, that and All That You Can't Leave Behind are my favourite U2 albums- granted, I think it's because they're the two I grew up with. And I even liked No Line On The Horizon , but that seems to never be talked about. It was definitely the album/moment where they quite heavily began to veer off into "phoning it in" territory. I'm sure some would argue that happened with my two favourite albums I mentioned above, but obviously my bias won't let me say that. I genuinely, thoroughly, enjoy almost every track on those two records. They make epic feel-good music which so many love and can vibe out to together, and there's great value in that, imo. Again, I'm obviously biased, but I genuinely can't fathom why the endless hate. It's funny when people will spew endless hate on them but always have the caveat "but their first few albums..."- it's just funny to observe the switch-up, from loving something to hating it so strongly. Moby is another one... I don't actually know whether he was actually widely loved or always kind of made fun of... I want to say Eminem alone did irreparable damage to the perception of Moby lol...but like, it seemed somewhat okay to say you liked him in the 2000's, whereas now, you're made to be some big lame if you do. As much as I'm for animal rights and don't deny his heart is in the right place with all that, it can definitely be heavy-handed and over-the-top. RHCP another one, similar to U2, where the first few albums, culminating in BSSM, are seen as something revolutionary/explosive/amazing, but anything later gets regularly put down. My personal favourite is the three record run of Californication-By The Way-Stadium Arcadium . Coldplay... they seemed to be made fun of from the start, for what, allegedly being a Radiohead rip-off/wannabe? Idk, they're def nowhere near Radiohead quality/status, but their first three or four albums are solid. I will admit, even as a fan, that anything post-Mylo Xyloto (and even that album) just sounds so overtly polished and devoid of soul. A big departure from the first few. See, even just writing all this out, I can already feel your hate and judgement coming a mile away, I've been so conditioned to be ashamed of my taste by fellow music fans, which is what the real lame thing is, imo. I'm just curious though what it is that makes certain once-loved acts become hated later. And I mean purely as far as the music goes- of course with the shitty things they've done in their personal lives, that's more than reason enough to forever hate on someone... but this hate was observed before many such things came to light- like there was some collective barometer reading "sellout". What is the sound of selling out? How does it appear/manifest in the music? Genuinely curious.

text: Is there an asymmetry to how music critics discuss “simple” and “complex” music? Technical virtuosity and emotional expression are often considered mutually exclusive ideas. I disagree. I would actually posit that prog, jazz, metal, or otherwise maximalist musicians are actually deeply passionate about what they do, often have something unique and profound to say, and are choosing to express themselves with a more advanced form of language, much like poets or playwrights. And rather than attacking the language outright, we should grant these musicians the same grace we extend to three-chord singer-songwriters and ambient synthesists, who are often considered more “honest” artists. What critics call “bloat” can actually serve distinct artistic purposes: Long-form composition can signify a vast journey, literally or metaphorically, and allow the writers ample time for motivic development. Shifting key centers or time signatures can indicate changes in mood or atmosphere. Use of atypical or mixed modes can communicate an unusual or “outsider” perspective. Maximalist arranging can take already large emotions and make them overwhelming. Exceeding the established limitations of musical convention can communicate a deep spiritual transcendence. And yet, often when an artist shows a level of ambition beyond what is “cool,” they are often hit with lazy shorthand words like “overwrought,” “self-indulgent,” or the worst offender “masturbatory.” Conversely, minimalism is granted profundity by default. Restraint is always seen as a sign of “maturity.” Records with a lot of emptier space leave a considerable amount of room for the listener to project their own feelings, increasing a sense of depth that may or may not already be there. This leads to a broader follow-up question: Should paid professional music critics have a better understanding of concepts like composition, arranging, and musicianship? Consider the absurdity of an NFL sportswriter who doesn't know the basic rules and regulations of football; or a food critic who couldn’t distinguish between common cooking methods or ingredients. Why do we allow music critics to feel everything out on vibes instead of insisting that they show a firm understanding about the building blocks of their chosen medium? EDIT: Really appreciate all the thoughtful and insightful replies here, whether we agreed or disagreed. I'm stepping away now, so if you reply to get a final word in, I guess it's the final word. I think I've made my position as clear as it can be in the comments.
label: Philosophical Discussion

The song came out in the pre internet year of 1985 and at the time a person only had so many options for in their search for answers in the romantic sphere. You might ask an advice column or but probably you would have someone in your life who you trusted, a friend or family member, and you would go to them and and try to use their knowledge to help you better understand your world. Today people in the same situation would almost certainly turn to the internet or AI and ask random strangers who don't know them and we they do not know to guess at the specifics of their love life and hope the people on the other end know what they hell they are talking about. text: Has music become less "daring" over the last years/decades? A few days ago, I asked myself the question if music had become less "daring" over the last decades, and I wondered if I just feel this, or if others feel this way too. But first, I want to explain how this question arised. Let us go back in time, back to the early 1960s. Rock'n'Roll was the big deal over in America, but then suddenly, a new group in the UK arises, breaking with a lot of traditions and typical ideas about music. I am talking about "The Beatles". The Beatles are among my favourite artists, and Revolver and Abbey Road are my favourite Beatles albums. Revolver was quite unique, too. A reversed guitar solo, tape effects etc. Only a few years later, prog-bands like King Crimson, ELP, Yes, Genesis and CAN emerged. They all pushed the boundaries of rock music in different directions. King Crimson especially in their 70s with LTIA and Red (but of course also in the 80s with their new-wave style), Yes and ELP in other, yet also not less interesting and "new" territories. At the same time, Germany brought out electronic music bands like Tangerine Dream and Kraftwerk, who both significantly shaped this new genre, while being successfull. Then, we had bands like Nirvana, that managed to make a more underground genre (grunge) popular, and became successfull. I could go on and list a lot of other artists, who didn't stick to the same musical ideas throughout their career, like Kate Bush, Tool, Talk Talk and of course David Bowie. And while we may have an Angine de Poitrine in 2026, artists which want to break out of established musical constructs have become a rarity, at least, those who are still somewhat successfull while doing this. If all of this is really true, and that music has become less courageous, one question still remains: why? What caused all of this to happen? Is it the omnipresent availabilty of music via streaming services? I don't know. I'd really be interested in how you see this.
label: Deep Analysis

text: The Foxes and almost making it Hi all, Has anyone ever heard of a band from the UK called The Foxes? They came out around 2006 and were an indie rock band. It was MySpace, after all, where you could just comment on a bands page and sometimes they’d just reply. On more than one occasion their singer, Nigel, responded to me. I remember them posting about potentially doing a US tour and while I never was able to go myself, they did do the tour. I found out recently that Nigel has been posting on [Substack](https://substack.com/@nigelthomaswriter?r=7unuck&utm_medium=ios&utm_source=stories&shareImageVariant=image) detailing the start of the band, getting scouted, being featured on MySpace and he’s currently up to the US Tour part of the story which I am so incredibly interested in since I didn’t get to experience it while it was happening! It’s fascinating seeing the process of « making it » through the bands eyes. Really unique, especially when I compare where I was at the time (ie encountering them on MySpace) versus his retelling of what was happening from the bands perspective. He’s also a wonderful writer. The way he tells it is entertaining and so very well thought out. He even includes diary entries - always humourous! Has anyone else ever seen something like this from a band? The behind the scenes bits are fascinating. I’d love to see if any other bands have done or written something similar? He still makes himself accessible for comments and things which blows me away. So unlike most bands I’ve seen. I feel like I’m always alone in knowing about them. Just curious if anyone else knows who they are? Anyone listened to them? Came across them on the myspace featured artists page? I’m so surprised they never took off here more, especially since I remember Franz Ferdinand being pretty well known! Oh, incase nobody knows what I’m talking about — check them out. They haven’t been together for years and years but I keep them on my playlist. If you’re into the mid 2000s post punk/indie scene from the UK give them a [listen.](https://youtube.com/@thefoxes?si=1FEKS8-dX7oDzvdR) My favourites are Lover, Killer and Trauma Town, personally !

text: Are Janet Jackson’s Control and Rhythm Nation 1814 actually stronger albums than Michael Jackson’s Bad and Dangerous? I’ve been thinking about Janet Jackson’s Control (1986) and Rhythm Nation 1814 (1989) compared with Michael Jackson’s Bad (1987) and Dangerous (1991). Michael obviously had the bigger global impact and some of the most iconic singles of all time, but if we judge them strictly as albums , I’m starting to wonder whether Janet’s records are actually stronger. Control feels incredibly focused, with a very clear identity and almost no wasted space. And Rhythm Nation 1814 might be even more impressive: conceptually coherent, socially ambitious, rhythmically innovative, and remarkably consistent from beginning to end. By comparison, Bad has enormous highs, but does it work as cohesively as Rhythm Nation ? And while Dangerous is adventurous and influential, I sometimes feel that it’s more uneven than either of Janet’s albums. So my question is: Would you rank Control and Rhythm Nation 1814 above Bad and Dangerous purely as albums, separate from sales, fame, music videos, and Michael Jackson’s cultural stature? I’d especially be interested in hearing comparisons involving songwriting, production, sequencing, consistency, innovation, and how well each album has aged.

text: The Disconnect Between Favorite Songs Of The 90s & Hit Singles Of The 90s The American radio station KEXP recently aired a countdown of KEXP Listeners’ Favorite Songs Of The 90s. It’s a good list to check out. However, the thing that struck me immediately is how some of these songs weren’t hits in their time - they were either slow burns that have accumulated fans over time or have been used in media after their release and have become notable. Here are the top 10 songs on the list [spoiler] followed by their chart performance in the US and UK. Beck “Loser” (US #10 / UK #15) Soundgarden “Black Hole Sun” (US - / UK #12) Radiohead “Creep” (US #34 / UK #7) Deee-Lite “Groove Is In The Heart” (US #4 / UK #2) Massive Attack “Teardrop” (US - / UK #10) Radiohead “Paranoid Android” (US - / UK #3) The Breeders “Cannonball” (US #44 / UK #40) Beastie Boys “Sabotage” (US - / UK #19) Mazzy Star “Fade Into You” (US #44 / UK #48) Nirvana “Smells Like Teen Spirit” (US #6 / UK #7) I’m not arguing against any of these picks, they are all great songs. What is fascinating to me how far away from hits that some of these songs were - “Cannonball” and “Fade Into You” in particular were not notable as singles but have grown in time to iconic 90s songs. Just for fun, the year 1994 is overrepresented in the top 10 above: four of the ten songs were released as singles in 1994. What were the top singles in the US and UK in 1994? “The Sign” by Ace Of Base and “Love Is All Around” by Wet Wet Wet. It’s worth noting: the listenership of KEXP skews older and more towards rock. That said, ask the same question on this sub and you might arrive at a similar answer. I’m interested to hear what people think about how favorite songs 30 years on differs so greatly from what was popular in its time. If you ask about favorites songs of the 90s in 20 years, will the answers change again?
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: How much can an album’s last track change the meaning of everything before it? I've been thinking about how much weight the final track of an album can carry. Sometimes an album seems to be telling you one story, but the ending makes you reconsider everything that came before it. A tragic ending can make earlier moments of confidence feel more like denial. A hopeful ending can make everything that seemed hopeless before it feel completely different. But I think there's a fine line between an ending that genuinely changes your perspective and one that feels forced. If the rest of the album hasn't earned that conclusion, even a beautiful final track might not be enough to make it convincing. And I'm not necessarily talking about albums where the closing track is the best song. I'm more interested in endings that change how you interpret the earlier tracks when you listen again. Have you ever experienced that with an album? What was it, and what specifically changed about how you heard the rest of it after reaching the end?
label: Philosophical Discussion

Spring is always a blast of fresh, upbeat pop or maybe some classic rock. Something that just makes you feel like opening the windows and going for a drive. That feeling of new beginnings. It's almost involuntary for me. And summer is definitely funk soul and reggae. Beach music. Anything with a good groove that makes you want to move. Super chill vibes for long warm evenings. text: Sophisti-pop, and other genres that have never had a revival One of my favorite musical discoveries in the last decade was Sophisti-pop. While the name is a bit, frankly, not great, the genre itself is absolutely stacked full of critically acclaimed artists and albums. Artists like China Crisis, Roxy Music, Prefab Sprout, Everything but the Girl's early work, Level 42, and my personal favorite, The Blue Nile. It's a very specific sound, and it emerged at a very specific point in time. It got moderately to very popular, depending on the artist (Sade was massive, for instance), but for all intents and purposes only practically existed between 1982 or 83 to around 1990, and fizzled back into the underground after. While other artists have played with this sound on songs here and there, like Blood Orange and Carly Rae Jepsen, it's never had a true revival at any point in time. So that got me thinking: What other notable 20 th century styles of music have never had a popular revival, even for a short period of time? Obviously, this isn't focused on a song or two that might have come out, but proper revivals, such as the swing and rockabilly revival in the mid 90's, or the disco and funk revival that happened at the end of the 2010's into the early 2020's.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Problem with concerts Hey guys! I am someone who really enjoys music. For that reason, you would assume I also like concerts. I have tried to go to a handful throughout the past years, and in almost all of them I end up being surrounded by people having full-on conversations! I feel that they go to the show because they know a couple of songs they want to listen to, and throughout the rest of the show they are just screaming with each other about Pilates classes. Yesterday was one of these cases, and, as much as I hate confrontation, after having these 2 ladies chat so loudly for the first 4 or 5 songs, I turned back and told them that it was really difficult to enjoy the show with them talking all the time. I was wondering how others feel about this? Do you still enjoy the show? Because to me it completely ruins the experience, and considering tickets cost a few hundred dollars… Maybe most people don’t mind, and I’m “the problem” and concerts are not for me, but the fact that these people are so self centered and selfish really blows my mind

text: I want to give a shout out to Swans’s gothic era! Took some time to go back to a couple of Swans albums. Revisited Children of God, White Light from the Mouth of Infinity & The Great Annihilator. Then I went back to Love of Life & The Burning World. And I have to say, this part of their career is very very interesting! I mean, what they pulled off on those albums is astounding when you consider the existence of Filth & Cop. Those two albums are like trying to dominate someone & succeeding….in the most brutal fashion that you could think of. Uncompromising, harsh, scary, full of rage & hate. The most pessimistic view of humanity that you could get. Reminded me of an extremely violent section of a bar that’s full of “FUCK YOU” graffiti. Someone shaking their fist at you & pounding you into submission until there’s blood left over. But My God….what Swans transformed into from Children of God to The Great Annihilator is unbelievable! There’s a constant mixture of darkness & beauty that’s really fascinating. Lush textures, ethereal keyboards, guitars that are elegant or luscious instead of “rip your face off”. So many lovely melodies. But there’s always an unsettling vibe. Embracing the macabre or disturbing parts of life. Haunting and luxurious at the same time. And I love the gothic/folky bits. Crazy how they pulled them off so well considering their No Wave/noise rock roots. Adding acoustic guitars into the mix, softening their style & going for “existential” rather than “violent”…..so awesome to me. Sorrowful but really captivating. There’s something about this era that reminded me of groups like the Velvet Underground, Joy Division & Leonard Cohen. Or even Wire/Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds. Great storytelling. Like you’re huddled around a bunch of people in a room, sharing their experiences late at night with the moon shingling through the window. I could totally include tracks from Children of God to The Great Annihilator in a playlist that has Bauhaus, the Cure, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Echo & the Bunnymen, etc. I really appreciate Jarboe’s contributions too! Hearing her vocals, seeing her songwriting credits & knowing that she played keyboard parts….I really like that. Gave a nice contrast to Michael Gira, added some variety. I think that Jarboe really emphasized that “darkness + beauty” thing that I mentioned earlier. Along with showing how much Swans changed from Filth & Cop. I like Soundtracks for the Blind & a lot of the post-reunion stuff too. But I think that the run from Children of God to The Great Annihilator deserves some love. Demonstrates that Swans is more than a crazy noise band haha!
